tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__visualize__show_widget
tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

schema.name: mcp__visualize__show_widget
schema.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). content.text:
Pull: already up to date, nothing new on `jusprin-newui`.

Commit `55a2d37618` ("Review print setup against user intent in core agent guidance", Oct 12) is a prompt-only change. It rewrites what the in-app assistant is told about preparing a print; no tool behaviour or schema changes.

**What it changes in the assistant's instructions**

- **Print journey guidance** ([ToolRegistry.hpp:33](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.hpp:33)): the four-line "how a print request goes" note becomes three sections.
  - **Intent and setup:** once the intended use is clear, assess the current material, filament preset and process preset against it. It must read the effective settings (including customizations and object overrides) rather than trust preset names, keep what already fits, and not repeat the assessment when nothing changed.
  - **Preparation:** advice requests get recommendations, not project changes. `plan_set` is only required for multi-change preparation; a clear single change can go straight to its tool.
  - **Verification:** slice and check with `slice_report` before reporting readiness. Starting a physical print still goes through the Send preflight and authorization.
- **Base system prompt** ([OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp:160](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp:160)): adds three rules.
  - Stay within the scope the user asked for; a question or troubleshooting does not authorize project changes.
  - A selected filament preset does not prove which spool is loaded.
  - An action starting is not evidence that it finished.

**Conflicting guidance it resolves**

- **`export_file`** ([ToolRegistry.cpp:1197](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp:1197)): the slice check now applies only to `gcode` and `sliced_3mf`; the other export kinds explicitly don't need one.
- **Printer panel** ([printerInstructions.ts:68](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts:68)): when guessing, it used to be told to ask first and call no tool. It may now use read-only tools to find candidates, then must ask and wait before adding, changing or connecting a printer.
- **MCP discovery instructions** ([McpProtocol.cpp:184](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp:184)): the inspect → preview → apply sequence is now scoped to "a requested settings change" rather than reading as a default workflow.

**Tests** ([test_openai_responses_agent.cpp](tests/agent/test_openai_responses_agent.cpp)): these cover the "prompt isolation" part of the message. The print guidance must appear in the main chat's instructions, must not appear in auto-title requests, and a panel with its own instructions gets exactly those. The instructions must also stay identical across tool continuations.

These things seem like the knowledge that agents should already have. But for whatever reason or the prompt was having a hard time to elicit Those expected actions. And when we Started piling up more and rules and instructions into core prompt as we did in 55a2d37618, The help was limited and Other edge cases started to fall apart.   

I suspect that we're doing something fundamentally wrong here. Is it because our core prompt are too complicated? Is it because we have been testing with a very uh a small model without reasoning? Or is it something completely different? Use your knowledge as well as search online to check for guidance about how situations like this should be handled.

The official OpenAI guide covers all three topics, though the search snippets cut off before its contradictions section, so I can't confirm its exact wording on that point.

**Agentic eagerness:** OpenAI describes this as the model's balance between taking initiative and waiting for explicit guidance. Agentic scaffolds range from systems that hand most decisions to the model to systems that keep it on a tight leash with heavy programmatic branching. GPT-5 is trained to work anywhere on that range. The guide also has a "prompting for less eagerness" section. Its example suggests setting different clarification thresholds per tool: a payment tool should require user confirmation more readily than a search tool, and a file-deletion tool should have a much lower threshold than a grep search tool (the checkout and payment tools should explicitly have a lower uncertainty threshold for requiring user clarification, while the search tool should have an extremely high threshold). A third-party summary adds that the guide recommends defining "early stop" criteria and giving the model an "escape hatch" (permission to proceed under uncertainty) to avoid over-searching.

**Tool preambles:** These are short statements the model makes before calling tools. One summary of the guide describes them as rephrasing goals, outlining plans, narrating progress, and summarizing results. A separate guide notes that in practice, the three levers that matter most are reasoning_effort, verbosity, and tool preambles.

**Instruction contradictions:** The search results only touch on this. A third-party commentary says contradictions force the model to reconcile conflicts instead of solving the task. The guide's own treatment of conflicting instructions didn't appear in the snippets, so check the original page for its specific advice.

**Rules pile up and compete.** One practitioner describes a code-review agent with forty rules in its system prompt. It respected file boundaries early, then broke them by turn four and five. The team traced the failures to rules that were present but had stopped being applied, and argued the core problem is that every rule sits in the same layer as tool output, documents, and user requests, all competing for one budget (a team puts forty repository rules into the system prompt, and the agent still edits temporary logs as if they were source files; every rule sits in the same layer, and rules, documents, state, memory, tool output, and user requests all compete for the same context budget).

**Each added instruction costs something.** One guide argues that a short system prompt matters because the death of model performance is by a thousand cuts. Each instruction you give the model degrades its performance. This is a practitioner heuristic, not a measured law.

**Position and conflicts matter.** The same guide says models tend to recall the start and end of a prompt best, so explicit instructions buried in the middle are often ignored. It also warns that multiple conflicting definitions of the same behavior (for example, three different definitions of "out-of-scope") leave the agent unable to tell what to do (almost all models recall best what is in the beginning and the end of the prompt, explicit, specific instructions in the middle are often forgotten).

**Tool count is a separate limit.** A secondhand summary of a Berkeley function-calling leaderboard reports that a quantized Llama 3.1 8B handled 19 tools but failed at 46, and frames the issue as complexity rather than context length (a quantized Llama 3.1 8B worked fine with 19 tools and fell apart at 46. The window had room; the model's discrimination didn't. Complexity, not length, was the killer.). I could not verify this against the leaderboard itself.

Anthropic's "Building effective agents" post draws a clear line between workflows and agents, and it argues for keeping systems as simple as possible. My search didn't find anything that directly addresses prompts accumulating rules, so that part of your question is only partly answered.

**Workflows vs. agents.** Anthropic groups all of these designs under "agentic systems" but separates two types. Workflows are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. Agents are different: the model itself decides its own steps and tool use. Put simply, workflows are fixed paths written in code, and agents leave routing decisions to the model.

**Start simple.** The guidance is to find the simplest solution possible, and only increase complexity when needed. The post also says this might mean not building agentic systems at all. One secondary summary notes that for many applications, optimising single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples suffices.

**Costs of agency.** Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, and you should consider when this tradeoff makes sense. A third-party write-up adds that each extra autonomous turn adds latency, token cost, and the chance that an early mistake propagates. That error-compounding point is the closest the results come to your concern about complexity piling up.

**Frameworks.** The post warns against reaching for frameworks by default. Its reasoning, as one summary describes it, is that they "often create extra layers of abstraction that can obscure the underling prompts and responses". That matters for your question: when rules pile up inside a framework, it becomes harder to see what the prompt actually says.

**What the search didn't cover.** None of the results discuss how to manage a growing set of prompt rules, such as when to split them into separate workflow steps, when to trim them, or how to test them. For that, I'd read the full post at anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents. The "Building effective agents" post is the primary source; the mer.vin and Substack pages are secondary summaries.

**API setup**
- OpenAI's guide recommends the Responses API for tool-calling and multi-turn work, so reasoning items carry across tool calls (Use the Responses API for reasoning, tool-calling, and multi-turn workflows so reasoning items can be preserved between tool calls.).
- The cookbook makes the same point, noting that reasoning is persisted between tool calls, leading to more efficient and intelligent outputs.

**Reasoning effort**
- The valid values are minimal, low, medium, and high.
- OpenAI suggests starting at medium and then testing other levels against your own representative tasks (Start with medium reasoning effort, then test minimal, low, or high against representative tasks.).
- To reduce unnecessary tool use and latency, lowering reasoning effort is the first lever OpenAI names (Switch to a lower reasoning_effort.).
- For mini specifically, one third-party summary says it is balanced speed and cost, ideal for chat and medium-difficulty reasoning.

**Controlling agentic eagerness**
- By default, GPT-5 is thorough and comprehensive when trying to gather context in an agentic environment, so prompts may need to rein it in.
- OpenAI's cookbook includes a sample spec for context gathering. It sets a goal of getting enough context quickly, fans out parallel searches, and gives explicit early-stop criteria, such as when the model can name the exact files to change (You can name exact files/symbols to change.).
- The troubleshooting guide also recommends an explicit stop condition and a self-check before the model replies (Give the assistant an explicit stop condition and a single, fast self-check before it replies.).

**Instruction following and system prompts**
- OpenAI says the model was trained to focus on improving tool calling, instruction following, and long-context understanding.
- Because it follows instructions closely, prompts should be precise. Third-party guidance notes that it can also make high-level decisions when instructions aren't clear.
- The official guide also advises re-testing prompts for agentic persistence, tool preambles, and stopping conditions.

**Tool preambles and verbosity**
- Preambles let the model explain its plan and progress before tool calls. The third-party write-up describes this as a way to give users better visibility into its process.

The search didn't turn up a direct comparison of encoding workflow in tools versus prompts, or of per-step subagents on small models in 2026. The sources are mostly practitioner blogs, so treat what follows as design guidance rather than benchmark evidence.

**What the sources support**

- **Compounding per-step error.** One blog gives the arithmetic: A two-step agent with 95% per-step accuracy lands at 90% end-to-end; a ten-step agent at the same per-step rate lands at 60%. This is the strongest argument for fewer, narrower decisions per step.
- **Fixed paths are more reliable.** One source describes a workflow as a predefined code path, while an Agent is driven by dynamic LLM decisions. It rates workflow reliability as high (deterministic path) and agent reliability as lower. Anthropic's guidance, as summarized there, is to start simple, add complexity only when necessary.
- **Handoffs lose state.** Agents passing context between each other lose information at every handoff. That cost applies to a subagent-per-step design.
- **Prompt-only agents are fragile.** One article says prompt-only agents often fail in production because they hallucinate parameters and struggle with multi-step tasks. Its claim that tool calling gives 41% higher completion rates cites a "LangChain 2026 Agent Report" that I could not verify, so don't rely on that number.
- **Long prompts degrade.** Encoding a long workflow in the system prompt has a cost. One source says effective capacity is 30–50% of the nominal for reasoning-heavy tasks, and this is a heuristic, not a measurement.
- **Reflection costs more.** Critic passes help, but the cost is doubled inference.
- **Small models.** One source describes mid-size open models fine-tuned for tool use and JSON output. Another suggests a split of a frontier planner and a cheaper executor.

**Practical reading (my inference, not from the sources)**

For small models, the evidence points toward moving the workflow out of the prompt and into code or graph control flow, with each step as a narrow, schema-validated tool or subagent call. The prompt then handles only per-step judgment. Keep the per-step decision space small, validate tool outputs, and cap retries. Whether a small model's per-step accuracy is high enough to justify this split should be measured on your own task.

**Gaps**

I didn't find controlled studies comparing these designs on small models. If you need that, search for τ-bench or BFCL results for small models, or papers on workflow-versus-agent comparisons, rather than practitioner posts.

58	Run every case, not only the one the edit is for. The three sessions share one
59	prompt, so a line written for one of them reaches the other two; a fix is one
60	whose own case improves while no other case drops.

62	Every reply in every case is also held to the rules the prompt sets for all
63	replies: a `Choices:` line the page draws as intended (on the last line, two
64	to four choices under 30 characters; read as
65	`replyChoices.ts` reads it), and none of the internal words the prompt rules
66	out (profile, preset, catalog, a tool's name). A reply that breaks one fails

70	Those ask a stronger model (`JUDGE_MODEL`, pinned) one narrow yes-or-no
71	question about the conversation's last reply, and the run prints its reason.

75	## What keeps it faithful to the app
76	
77	- **The system prompt and the opening line** come from the page's own source,
78	  through `render_prompt.mjs` and the page's esbuild. This needs node and the
79	  AgentUI npm install.
80	- **`printer_tools.json`** is the tool list the app sends in the printer panel.
81	  `test_openai_responses_agent.cpp` fails when it drifts from the registry.
82	  Regenerate it with
83	  `JUSPRIN_UPDATE_PRINTER_TOOLS=1 agent_bridge_tests '[printer]'`.
84	- **The chat history** is built the way `AgentHost` and `OpenAIResponsesAgent`
85	  build it: each earlier assistant message's words, then the tool calls it
86	  made with their results (replayed since `jusprin-newui` 115e2776bf); then
87	  this turn's message, tool calls and results. A call the app refused before
88	  it ran is not replayed, because the app never recorded it.

90	  printer, recorded from a real run.

93	answers them is the one prompts are evaluated on, not necessarily the one the

96	## Cases
97	
98	- `connect-bambu`: connect a saved Bambu Lab A1 mini that is on the network.
99	  Passes when the model opens `printer_connect`'s credential form for it. Before the app
100	  replayed earlier tool results, it failed about a third of the time: the model
101	  looked up the printer's id in one turn, and on "connect it" in the next it had
102	  no id and invented one, such as `<from_status>`.
103	
104	- `add-named-model`: the person names one model ("bambu lab a1 mini"). Passes
105	  when that printer is added and the reply ends with the connect offer the
106	  prompt spells out, "Want to connect it so you can send prints straight to
107	  it?", with the choices Connect it and Not now.
108	- `add-choose-from-three`: "prusa mk4" fits three models, then the person
109	  chooses "Prusa MK4S". Passes when nothing is added before the choice, the
110	  chosen printer is, and the reply ends with the connect offer. A second
111	  lookup of the chosen printer draws a second picture card; it is reported,
112	  not failed.
113	
114	- `add-then-undo`: the person names one model, it is added, then they tap Undo
115	  on its receipt. The app removes it, posts its note as a developer message,
116	  and starts a turn with nothing said (`PrinterConversation::undo_add`).
117	  Passes when that reply adds nothing, drops the connect offer and asks which
118	  printer they have. Without the prompt's rule about undone adds it passed 3 of
119	  20 (2026-09-24): the model mostly said "Okay, it's removed" and stopped, and
120	  some replies said "I removed" as if it had.
121	- `add-not-now-close`, `connect-verified-close`, `connect-leave-close`,
122	  `change-nozzle-close`: the four places the prompt says nothing is left to
123	  decide -- the person turns down connecting, the app's note says the
124	  connection is verified, they leave a failed connection for now, a nozzle
125	  change is saved. Each passes when that reply says the person can close the
126	  chat and offers no reply choices. The connect cases tap
127	  Submit the credential form and deliver the app's note as the app does: a developer
128	  message and no user message.
129	The cases above follow the main paths. The ones below are the rest of what
130	people say in each session -- questions the tools cannot answer, facts that
131	need nothing saved, requests that belong to another session -- and each checks
132	what must not happen as well as what should. The Change and Connect ones
133	answer the tools as `PrinterConversation` does for one saved printer
134	  (`SavedPrinterCase`), including its refusals (`preflight_tool`: no finding or
135	  adding outside an Add conversation, no change to another printer, no settings
136	  but that printer's), and fail on any call that adds, changes, connects or
137	  applies a settings change when that is not what was asked. The settings
138	tools read and check a fixed set of that printer's settings, as
139	`OrcaWorkspaceAdapter` answers for them: the printer is not the one the
140	project uses, so a change without `persistAs` is `not_selected`; a stock
141	profile (`stock`) refuses saving over itself with `read_only_preset`; bed size
142	and nozzle size are read-only.
143	
144	- Change, about a saved Anycubic Kobra 3 (a print host, not connected):
145	  - `change-add-another`: "I also have a Prusa MK4S, can you add it too?" The
146	    app refuses adding here, so trying is not a failure; the reply is. Passes
147	    when it says another printer is added from Home and does not say this one
148	    was added. It measures whether the model recovers from the refusal, which
149	    is what would justify offering fewer tools in a Change conversation.
150	  - `change-ask-start-gcode`: "what's the current start g-code?" Passes when
151	    it is read with `settings_get` and quoted. Fails when the reply treats the
152	    printer as not yet added, says the setting needs a network connection (it
153	    is on this computer), or asks which printer this is. Reported 2026-09-28,
154	    before the settings tools were offered here: a reply offered to add the
155	    printer, and another, about a Bambu Lab A1's z offset, asked "Which printer
156	    is it?". That z-offset conversation passed 10 of 10 on DeepSeek with the
157	    split prompt, so it has no case of its own.
158	  - `change-edit-start-gcode`: "add G29 right after the G28 line in the start
159	    g-code". Passes when the change is applied and saved under the printer's
160	    own name, with G29 after G28.
161	  - `change-bed-size`: "make the bed 250 by 250", which the settings tools
162	    refuse. Passes when nothing is changed and the reply says the person can
163	    change it in the app's printer settings, without claiming to open them.
164	  - `change-ask-nozzle`: "what nozzle size is it set up for?" Passes when the
165	    reply says 0.4.
166	  - `change-loaded-filament`, `change-plate`: a spool loaded, a plate swapped.
167	    Passes when nothing is saved.
168	  - `change-unshipped-nozzle`: "I put a 0.3 nozzle on it". Passes when nothing
169	    is saved and the reply names 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8.
170	  - `change-then-connect`: "can you connect it…?", then the address. Passes
171	    when the card opens for that address and no address was made up first.
172	- Change, about the settings OrcaSlicer ships for the Bambu Lab A1 mini,
173	  selected in the project (the header's Printer settings… on a project that
174	  uses them): `change-stock-copy`, "set the retraction length to 1 mm". Passes
175	  when the change is applied and saved as `Bambu Lab A1 mini 0.4 nozzle - Copy`,
176	  the copy `read_only_preset` suggests.
177	- Change, about a connected Bambu Lab A1 mini holding PLA and PETG:
178	  `change-ask-loaded`, "what filament is loaded right now?" Passes when the
179	  reply names both.
180	- Connect:
181	  - `connect-host-address`: a Voron given as "http://voron.local, I open it
182	    with Mainsail". Passes when the card opens for Moonraker at that address.
183	  - `connect-bambu-not-found`: no A1 mini in LAN mode on the network. Passes
184	    when the status is checked, no card opens, and the reply points to LAN
185	    mode or asks what the screen shows.
186	  - `connect-ask-why`: "do I have to connect it?" Passes when the reply says
187	    it is optional.
188	- Add:
189	  - `add-vague-description`: "the small bambu one". Passes when nothing is
190	    added before the person confirms.
191	  - `add-unsupported-printer`: a resin printer. Passes when nothing is shown
192	    or added and no other model is offered in its place.

194	Regressions: behaviour an earlier prompt or tool change fixed, found in the
195	history of `printerInstructions.ts` and the tools' wording. Each names the
196	commit that measured the failure, so a later edit made for something else
197	cannot quietly undo it.
198	
199	- `add-many-fit`: "prusa" (7f66e75b07: the model tried to show more than three
200	  printers 33 times). Passes when no printer is looked up or added and the
201	  reply narrows it down or offers the full list.
202	- `add-name-starts-two`: "bambu a1", which begins the A1 and the A1 mini
203	  (7f66e75b07: 0 of 3 with the rule in place). Passes when nothing is added and
204	  the reply asks which. Its A1 answer is written from the profile, not
205	  recorded.

208	  when nothing is saved and the reply names the sizes and asks the person to

211	  says the person can browse it manually in the app, without claiming to open
212	  it or adding a printer. The earlier test required a tool to open the list;
213	  that result is not comparable after removing the tool.

226	`printer_identify` and `printer_add` returned for the printers the cases name.

228	catalog or those tools' answers change.

230	A new case is a class in `run_prompt_tests.py` that has a session payload, a
231	`tool()` that answers calls, and a `run()` that says the person's lines and
232	returns the outcome. Add it to `CASES`.

234	## Which model
235	
236	The default is `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` on OpenRouter, pinned to Alibaba,
237	Novita, Baidu and AtlasCloud (`MODEL`, `PROVIDERS`). It was chosen on
238	2026-09-28 from four models run on these cases (29 then), three runs each, all
239	judged by the same `JUDGE_MODEL`:
240	
241	| Model | Passed |
242	|---|---|
243	| xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-pro, hosts Xiaomi and GMICloud | 85/87 |
244	| gpt-5.4-mini (the app's) | 82/87 |
245	| deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash, pinned hosts | 79/87 |
246	| minimax/minimax-m3, hosts AtlasCloud and DeepInfra | 72/87 |

248	This measures the prompt, not the provider a person's app is set up with.
249	`--model`, `--endpoint`, `--key-env` and `--provider` try another model through
250	a Responses API endpoint, to compare models rather than to judge a prompt
251	change, such as:
252	
253	```bash

256	```
257	
258	A model other than the default starts with no hosts pinned. The judge stays on
259	OpenAI whichever model answers, so counts are judged alike.
260	
261	Pin OpenRouter's hosts with `--provider` (repeatable). OpenRouter serves an
262	open-weight model from many hosts, and they render a message the model was not
263	trained on differently. The app's notes are `developer` messages, OpenAI's
264	convention: DeepSeek V4 has no such role in ordinary chat, and hosts that treat

269	model's hosts with a note as the last message before trusting its counts.
270	
271	## The filament chat's cases (2026-09-29)
272	
273	A filament chat about Bambu PLA Basic @BBL X1C, a filament OrcaSlicer ships
274	with two nozzle temperatures (one per nozzle kind), in slot 1
275	(`FilamentCase`, answered as `PrinterPanel::filament_preflight` and the
276	adapter answer): the settings tools alone, and a refusal of any other target
277	or of an apply without `persistAs`.
278	
279	- `filament-hotter`: "make the nozzle 5 degrees hotter". Passes when the
280	  temperature is read first and 225,225 is applied for every layer, saved
281	  as the copy the facts name.
282	- `filament-ask-temperature`: "what nozzle temperature does it print at?"
283	  Passes when it is read and 220 is said, with no change.
284	- `filament-other-settings`: "also make the walls thicker". Passes when no
285	  change is applied and the reply says the print's settings are changed elsewhere.
286	- `filament-own-in-place`: a filament the person saved ("My PLA"), "lower the
287	  nozzle temperature to 210". Passes when 210,210 is applied for every
288	  layer, saved under its own name.

290	20 runs each: 19, 20, 20 and 20. The miss said "preset" before a tool call.
291	Before the rule that a temperature without layers named is every layer's,
292	the model asked whether the first layer should change too (6 and 12 of 20);
293	before it was told to say "settings", 5 of 20 replies said "preset" or
294	"profile". `--prompt-rev` does not apply to these cases before the commit
295	that adds `filamentInstructions.ts`.
296	
297	## Baseline after offering the settings tools (2026-09-29)
298	
299	The printer panel now also offers `settings_search`, `settings_get`,
300	`settings_preview_patch` and `settings_apply_patch`, answered by
301	`SavedPrinterCase.settings` as the app answers them. Change and Connect
302	sessions get a scope rule that includes a printer's settings and a section of
303	settings rules; a stock profile's facts name the copy a change is saved as
304	(`copyName`). The Add prompt is unchanged, though Add sessions are offered the
305	same tools. Full suite, three runs per case, beside the previous prompt
306	(`--prompt-rev HEAD`) with the same tools on the same hosts:
307	
308	| Case | Previous prompt | This prompt |
309	|---|---|---|
310	| `change-ask-start-gcode` | 1 | 3 |
311	| `change-edit-start-gcode` | 0 | 1 |
312	| `change-stock-copy` | 0 | 3 |
313	| every other case, together | 82/87 | 83/87 |
314	
315	The other cases' misses were single runs on both sides, mostly in different
316	cases, which is noise at three runs. Each settings case alone, 20 runs:
317	`change-ask-start-gcode` 20 and 20, `change-edit-start-gcode` 20 and 19 (the
318	miss said "preset"), `change-bed-size` 19 and 20 (the miss was this runner crashing on a string
319	`target`, since fixed), `change-stock-copy` 20 and
320	20 once the facts named the copy -- 11 before, when the model had to learn the
321	name from `read_only_preset` and often invented one.
322	
323	DeepSeek V4 Flash sometimes sends `target` as a string of JSON. It comes in
324	bursts: in one full run both `change-edit-start-gcode` failures were eight
325	such calls in a row, while a later batch of 80 conversations had one, which
326	the model then sent correctly. The registry now says so when it happens
327	("target must be a JSON object, not a string holding one"); too few string
328	targets have been seen since to measure whether that ends the bursts.
329	
330	## Historical baseline before removing the dialog and finish tools
331	
332	The prompt before this tool removal, recorded in `dd7ca1b8ef`, run alongside
333	the one before it on 2026-09-28, three runs per case, with the app's refusals in place
334	(`PrinterConversation::preflight_tool`). The edit adds one sentence to the
335	Change and Connect scope rule: another printer is added with + Add printer on
336	Home. Every case not listed passed 3 of 3 in both runs.
337	
338	| Case | Before | After |
339	|---|---|---|
340	| `add-many-fit` | 0 | 1 |
341	| `add-name-starts-two` | 2 | 2 |
342	| `add-not-now-done` | 3 | 1 |
343	| `add-then-undo` | 2 | 2 |
344	| `add-unsupported-printer` | 2 | 3 |
345	| `change-add-another` | 1 | 3 |
346	| `change-nozzle-done` | 3 | 2 |
347	| **Total** | **78/87** | **79/87** |
348	
349	The Add rows differ by noise alone: the Add prompt is the same on both sides.
350	The `change-nozzle-done` drop is a Done offered beside another choice, seen
351	before the edit. `change-add-another` alone, 20 runs: 15 before and 20 after.
352	`change-ask-start-gcode` alone, 20 runs, before this edit: 20.
353	`add-name-starts-two` still fails in most runs: on "bambu a1" the model picks
354	the A1 without asking about the A1 mini.

# Printer panel prompt tests

The printer panel's assistant is a system prompt
(`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`), five printer
tools and the four settings tools, and the chat. The header's filament chat
is the same panel with its own prompt (`filamentInstructions.ts`) and the
settings tools alone; its cases are the `filament-*` ones. `run_prompt_tests.py` sends the live model the same
requests the app sends. It answers the tools the way the app answers them for
a fixed printer, then checks what the model did. The app does not run.

On Kenneth's local machine, the keys are in
`~/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env` (outside the repository, mode `600`). An
agent running this suite can load them for that command in a subshell:

```bash
( . "$HOME/.config/jusprin/prompt-test.env"; tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py )
```

Do not print, copy into the repository, or include the key values in a command
or test log. The file exports `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`; the
runner reads them from its environment.

Prompt changes are evaluated on DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter, served
only by the hosts that answer the app's notes, and on no other model (decided
2026-09-28; see "Which model"). `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` is for that model,
`OPENAI_API_KEY` for the judge.

A run is one sample of a model that answers differently each time, so each case
runs several times, in parallel, and reports a count. By default one invocation
runs at most 100 conversations (`RUN_BUDGET`), shared by the cases it runs: 2
each for the 36 cases, and at most 20 for a case run alone. `--runs N` sets
the count per case instead; use it to look closer at one case. By default
every run must pass; `--must-pass N` lowers the bar. `--verbose` prints every
conversation, not only the failed ones.

## Judging a prompt change

Run the cases before and after the edit and compare the counts; "Baseline"
below has the counts to start from. The script renders the prompt from the
TypeScript source on every run, so nothing needs building. At the default
three runs a case catches a behaviour that fails often, not one that fails one
time in twenty; when a case fails, or to judge the edit it was written for,
run that case alone, where it gets 20 runs.
Differences of a few runs out of 20 are noise; look for a clear gap.

For a prompt-only edit, run the previous prompt with `--prompt-rev HEAD` (any
git revision works): the page's source is read as it was there, and the checkout
is left alone. The current change also removes three tools, so the earlier
prompt and tool list are no longer a valid control for the affected cases.
Run both versions at the same time when their tools and case expectations match,
so both meet the same hosts and the same day. A baseline recorded earlier is a
guide, not a control: the same prompt
scored 76, 76 and 74 of 84 in three runs, so compare against a before run made
alongside the after run.
Paired this way, a real effect shows plainly: on 2026-09-28 a two-line edit
took `add-not-now-done` from 19 to 3 of 20 while its own case improved.

Run every case, not only the one the edit is for. The three sessions share one
prompt, so a line written for one of them reaches the other two; a fix is one
whose own case improves while no other case drops.

Every reply in every case is also held to the rules the prompt sets for all
replies: a `Choices:` line the page draws as intended (on the last line, two
to four choices under 30 characters; read as

its run, whatever the case checks.

answers them is the one prompts are evaluated on, not necessarily the one the
app is configured with (see "Which model").

  - `change-ask-start-gcode`: "what's the current start g-code?" Passes when
    it is read with `settings_get` and quoted. Fails when the reply treats the
    printer as not yet added, says the setting needs a network connection (it
    is on this computer), or asks which printer this is. Reported 2026-09-28,
    before the settings tools were offered here: a reply offered to add the
    printer, and another, about a Bambu Lab A1's z offset, asked "Which printer
    is it?". That z-offset conversation passed 10 of 10 on DeepSeek with the
    split prompt, so it has no case of its own.
  - `change-edit-start-gcode`: "add G29 right after the G28 line in the start
    g-code". Passes when the change is applied and saved under the printer's
    own name, with G29 after G28.
  - `change-bed-size`: "make the bed 250 by 250", which the settings tools
    refuse. Passes when nothing is changed and the reply says the person can
    change it in the app's printer settings, without claiming to open them.
  - `change-ask-nozzle`: "what nozzle size is it set up for?" Passes when the
    reply says 0.4.
  - `change-loaded-filament`, `change-plate`: a spool loaded, a plate swapped.
    Passes when nothing is saved.
  - `change-unshipped-nozzle`: "I put a 0.3 nozzle on it". Passes when nothing
    is saved and the reply names 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8.
  - `change-then-connect`: "can you connect it…?", then the address. Passes
    when the card opens for that address and no address was made up first.
- Change, about the settings OrcaSlicer ships for the Bambu Lab A1 mini,
  selected in the project (the header's Printer settings… on a project that
  uses them): `change-stock-copy`, "set the retraction length to 1 mm". Passes
  when the change is applied and saved as `Bambu Lab A1 mini 0.4 nozzle - Copy`,
  the copy `read_only_preset` suggests.
- Change, about a connected Bambu Lab A1 mini holding PLA and PETG:
  `change-ask-loaded`, "what filament is loaded right now?" Passes when the
  reply names both.
- Connect:
  - `connect-host-address`: a Voron given as "http://voron.local, I open it
    with Mainsail". Passes when the card opens for Moonraker at that address.
  - `connect-bambu-not-found`: no A1 mini in LAN mode on the network. Passes
    when the status is checked, no card opens, and the reply points to LAN
    mode or asks what the screen shows.
  - `connect-ask-why`: "do I have to connect it?" Passes when the reply says
    it is optional.
- Add:
  - `add-vague-description`: "the small bambu one". Passes when nothing is
    added before the person confirms.
  - `add-unsupported-printer`: a resin printer. Passes when nothing is shown
    or added and no other model is offered in its place.

Regressions: behaviour an earlier prompt or tool change fixed, found in the
history of `printerInstructions.ts` and the tools' wording. Each names the
commit that measured the failure, so a later edit made for something else
cannot quietly undo it.

- `add-many-fit`: "prusa" (7f66e75b07: the model tried to show more than three
  printers 33 times). Passes when no printer is looked up or added and the
  reply narrows it down or offers the full list.
- `add-name-starts-two`: "bambu a1", which begins the A1 and the A1 mini
  (7f66e75b07: 0 of 3 with the rule in place). Passes when nothing is added and
  the reply asks which. Its A1 answer is written from the profile, not
  recorded.
- `add-unshipped-nozzle`, and `change-unshipped-nozzle` above: a size the model
  does not ship (3633478c0e: the model listed the sizes and stopped). Passes
  when nothing is saved and the reply names the sizes and asks the person to
  check the nozzle.
- `add-full-list`: "show me the full printer list". Passes when the assistant
  says the person can browse it manually in the app, without claiming to open
  it or adding a printer. The earlier test required a tool to open the list;
  that result is not comparable after removing the tool.
- `change-ask-loaded-not-connected`: what is loaded on a printer that is not
  connected (492fdb5531). Passes when no filament is claimed as loaded.
- `connect-failed-ways-forward`: a print host that does not respond
  (c922876c66: a failure ended with no way forward). Passes when the initial
  reply says how long it can take and the failure reply names the three ways
  forward.
- `connect-bambu-no-plugin`: connecting without Bambu's network plug-in
  (e2e1c6e7cc: "isn't available right now" with no reason). Passes when no
  credential form opens and the reply gives the plug-in as the reason.

The add cases use `add_session.json`, recorded from a `--printer-live` run: the
Add session the page was sent, including the full printer list, and what
`printer_identify` and `printer_add` returned for the printers the cases name.
Nothing checks that this recording stays current; record it again when the
catalog or those tools' answers change.

A new case is a class in `run_prompt_tests.py` that has a session payload, a
`tool()` that answers calls, and a `run()` that says the person's lines and
returns the outcome. Add it to `CASES`.

## Which model

The default is `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` on OpenRouter, pinned to Alibaba,
Novita, Baidu and AtlasCloud (`MODEL`, `PROVIDERS`). It was chosen on
2026-09-28 from four models run on these cases (29 then), three runs each, all
judged by the same `JUDGE_MODEL`:

| Model | Passed |
|---|---|
| xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-pro, hosts Xiaomi and GMICloud | 85/87 |
| gpt-5.4-mini (the app's) | 82/87 |
| deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash, pinned hosts | 79/87 |
| minimax/minimax-m3, hosts AtlasCloud and DeepInfra | 72/87 |

This measures the prompt, not the provider a person's app is set up with.
`--model`, `--endpoint`, `--key-env` and `--provider` try another model through
a Responses API endpoint, to compare models rather than to judge a prompt
change, such as:

```bash
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... OPENAI_API_KEY=... tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py \
    --model xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-pro --provider Xiaomi --provider GMICloud
```

A model other than the default starts with no hosts pinned. The judge stays on
OpenAI whichever model answers, so counts are judged alike.

Pin OpenRouter's hosts with `--provider` (repeatable). OpenRouter serves an
open-weight model from many hosts, and they render a message the model was not
trained on differently. The app's notes are `developer` messages, OpenAI's
convention: DeepSeek V4 has no such role in ordinary chat, and hosts that treat
it as a `system` message open no reply turn after it, so the model answers an
app note with nothing or with noise (2026-09-28: StreamLake, Parasail and Relace
empty 3 of 3, DeepInfra junk; Alibaba, Novita, Baidu and AtlasCloud correct).
Unpinned, those cases measure which host a request landed on. Check a new
model's hosts with a note as the last message before trusting its counts.

## The filament chat's cases (2026-09-29)

A filament chat about Bambu PLA Basic @BBL X1C, a filament OrcaSlicer ships
with two nozzle temperatures (one per nozzle kind), in slot 1
(`FilamentCase`, answered as `PrinterPanel::filament_preflight` and the
adapter answer): the settings tools alone, and a refusal of any other target
or of an apply without `persistAs`.

- `filament-hotter`: "make the nozzle 5 degrees hotter". Passes when the
  temperature is read first and 225,225 is applied for every layer, saved
  as the copy the facts name.
- `filament-ask-temperature`: "what nozzle temperature does it print at?"
  Passes when it is read and 220 is said, with no change.
- `filament-other-settings`: "also make the walls thicker". Passes when no
  change is applied and the reply says the print's settings are changed elsewhere.
- `filament-own-in-place`: a filament the person saved ("My PLA"), "lower the
  nozzle temperature to 210". Passes when 210,210 is applied for every
  layer, saved under its own name.

20 runs each: 19, 20, 20 and 20. The miss said "preset" before a tool call.
Before the rule that a temperature without layers named is every layer's,
the model asked whether the first layer should change too (6 and 12 of 20);
before it was told to say "settings", 5 of 20 replies said "preset" or
"profile". `--prompt-rev` does not apply to these cases before the commit
that adds `filamentInstructions.ts`.

## Baseline after offering the settings tools (2026-09-29)

The printer panel now also offers `settings_search`, `settings_get`,
`settings_preview_patch` and `settings_apply_patch`, answered by
`SavedPrinterCase.settings` as the app answers them. Change and Connect
sessions get a scope rule that includes a printer's settings and a section of
settings rules; a stock profile's facts name the copy a change is saved as
(`copyName`). The Add prompt is unchanged, though Add sessions are offered the
same tools. Full suite, three runs per case, beside the previous prompt
(`--prompt-rev HEAD`) with the same tools on the same hosts:

| Case | Previous prompt | This prompt |
|---|---|---|
| `change-ask-start-gcode` | 1 | 3 |
| `change-edit-start-gcode` | 0 | 1 |
| `change-stock-copy` | 0 | 3 |
| every other case, together | 82/87 | 83/87 |

The other cases' misses were single runs on both sides, mostly in different
cases, which is noise at three runs. Each settings case alone, 20 runs:
`change-ask-start-gcode` 20 and 20, `change-edit-start-gcode` 20 and 19 (the
miss said "preset"), `change-bed-size` 19 and 20 (the miss was this runner crashing on a string
`target`, since fixed), `change-stock-copy` 20 and
20 once the facts named the copy -- 11 before, when the model had to learn the
name from `read_only_preset` and often invented one.

DeepSeek V4 Flash sometimes sends `target` as a string of JSON. It comes in
bursts: in one full run both `change-edit-start-gcode` failures were eight
such calls in a row, while a later batch of 80 conversations had one, which
the model then sent correctly. The registry now says so when it happens
("target must be a JSON object, not a string holding one"); too few string
targets have been seen since to measure whether that ends the bursts.

## Historical baseline before removing the dialog and finish tools

The prompt before this tool removal, recorded in `dd7ca1b8ef`, run alongside
the one before it on 2026-09-28, three runs per case, with the app's refusals in place
(`PrinterConversation::preflight_tool`). The edit adds one sentence to the
Change and Connect scope rule: another printer is added with + Add printer on
Home. Every case not listed passed 3 of 3 in both runs.

| Case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `add-many-fit` | 0 | 1 |
| `add-name-starts-two` | 2 | 2 |
| `add-not-now-done` | 3 | 1 |
| `add-then-undo` | 2 | 2 |
| `add-unsupported-printer` | 2 | 3 |
| `change-add-another` | 1 | 3 |
| `change-nozzle-done` | 3 | 2 |
| **Total** | **78/87** | **79/87** |

The Add rows differ by noise alone: the Add prompt is the same on both sides.
The `change-nozzle-done` drop is a Done offered beside another choice, seen
before the edit. `change-add-another` alone, 20 runs: 15 before and 20 after.
`change-ask-start-gcode` alone, 20 runs, before this edit: 20.
`add-name-starts-two` still fails in most runs: on "bambu a1" the model picks
the A1 without asking about the A1 mini.

**System prompt altitude**

- **Too brittle:** Engineers sometimes hardcode complicated rules to force exact behavior. The article says: "At one extreme, we see engineers hardcoding complex, brittle logic in their prompts to elicit exact agentic behavior." This creates fragility and maintenance overhead.
- **Too vague:** Other prompts give high-level guidance without concrete signals, or assume shared context the model doesn't have.
- **Right altitude:** The goal is a middle ground. "The optimal altitude strikes a balance: specific enough to guide behavior effectively," while still leaving the model room to apply good heuristics.

**Recommended structure**

Organize prompts into distinct sections, such as background information, instructions, tool guidance, and output description. Use XML tags or Markdown headers to separate them. The article notes that exact formatting may matter less as models improve.

**Minimal set of information**

Aim for the smallest set of information that fully describes the expected behavior. "Minimal" doesn't necessarily mean short. Start with a minimal prompt on the best available model, then add instructions and examples to fix failures you observe.

**Tool design**

- Tools define the agent's contract with its environment, so they should return token-efficient information.
- Each tool should be self-contained, robust to errors, and clearly scoped, with minimal overlap.
- Bloated tool sets with ambiguous choices are a common failure. The article suggests that if a human can't clearly pick the right tool, the agent won't either.

**Examples**

Rather than listing every edge case in the prompt, curate a small set of diverse, canonical examples that show the expected behavior. The article describes examples as the "pictures" worth a thousand words.

**Main recommendations**

- **Choose tools deliberately.** Don't just wrap existing API endpoints. Build a few tools for high-impact workflows, and consolidate multi-step operations into one call. For example, a single scheduling tool can replace separate user, event, and creation calls. Quote: "More tools don't always lead to better outcomes."

- **Namespace tools.** Group related tools under shared prefixes by service and resource so agents can tell them apart. Test whether prefix or suffix naming works better for your model. Quote: "Namespacing (grouping related tools under common prefixes) can help delineate boundaries between lots of tools;"

- **Return meaningful context.** Return high-signal, human-readable information and avoid low-level identifiers. A `response_format` option (concise or detailed) lets agents choose the level of detail. Quote: "They should prioritize contextual relevance over flexibility,"

- **Optimize for token efficiency.** Limit large responses with pagination, filtering, or truncation, and use sensible defaults. Make errors actionable rather than opaque. Quote: "implementing some combination of pagination, range selection, filtering, and/or truncation"

- **Prompt-engineer tool descriptions.** Write descriptions as if onboarding a new hire, and make parameter names unambiguous (such as `user_id` rather than `user`). Quote: "Avoid ambiguity by clearly describing (and enforcing with strict data models) expected inputs and outputs."

- **Run an evaluation loop.**
  - Build prototypes and test them yourself.
  - Create evaluation tasks from realistic workflows. Quote: "Strong evaluation tasks might require multiple tool calls—potentially dozens."
  - Use verifiers that tolerate harmless formatting differences.
  - Track accuracy, tool calls, runtime, tokens, and errors.
  - Read agent reasoning and transcripts to find friction.
  - Have an agent refine the tools, and check against held-out test sets to avoid overfitting. Quote: "Claude is an expert at analyzing transcripts and refactoring lots of tools all at once"

**1. Instruction contradictions**
- "poorly-constructed prompts containing contradictory or vague instructions can be more damaging to GPT-5 than to other models"
- "it expends reasoning tokens searching for a way to reconcile the contradictions rather than picking one instruction at random"
- Effect: resolving the conflicts yields more efficient reasoning. The guide says "By resolving the instruction hierarchy conflicts, GPT-5 elicits much more efficient and performant reasoning."
- Review advice: "removing them drastically streamlined and improved their GPT-5 performance," and the guide recommends testing prompts in the prompt optimizer tool to find such issues.

**2. Controlling agentic eagerness**
- *Less eager:* Lower `reasoning_effort`. Define clear exploration criteria. Set tool-call budgets if you want maximal prescriptiveness. Provide an escape hatch, such as "even if it might not be fully correct."
- *More eager:* "we recommend increasing `reasoning_effort`, and using a prompt like the following to encourage persistence"
- Persistence prompt: "please keep going until the user's query is completely resolved, before ending your turn and yielding back to the user."
- Also: "Never stop or hand back to the user when you encounter uncertainty." Clearly state stop conditions, and define safe versus unsafe actions and when handing back is acceptable. Higher-stakes tools should have lower thresholds for asking the user.

**3. reasoning_effort for agentic tool calling**
- "the default is `medium`, but you should scale up or down depending on the difficulty of your task."
- "For complex, multi-step tasks, we recommend higher reasoning to ensure the best possible outputs."
- "Many workflows can be accomplished with consistent results at medium or even low `reasoning_effort`."
- Peak performance comes when separable tasks are split across agent turns, one task per turn.

**4. Minimal reasoning**
- "We consider this to be the best upgrade for latency-sensitive users, as well as current users of GPT-4.1."
- Use prompting patterns similar to GPT-4.1. "minimal reasoning performance can vary more drastically depending on prompt than higher reasoning levels"
- Key points: ask for a brief summary of reasoning at the start of the answer; request thorough tool preambles; disambiguate tool instructions and add persistence reminders; and use prompted planning, since the model has fewer reasoning tokens for internal planning.

**5. Prompt length, over-specification, and metaprompting**
- Over-specification can backfire. Cursor found a "maximize_" thoroughness instruction "counterproductive with GPT-5, which is already naturally introspective and proactive at gathering context." Softening it reduced unnecessary tool use.
- Structured, scoped prompts "yield the most reliable results," per Cursor's testing.
- Markdown drift in long conversations: re-append a Markdown instruction "every 3-5 user messages."
- Metaprompting: "early testers have found great success using GPT-5 as a meta-prompter for itself." Ask "what elements could be added to an unsuccessful prompt to elicit a desired behavior, or removed to prevent an undesired one."
- Keep edits minimal: "While keeping as much of the existing prompt intact as possible" is the template's guidance.
